rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the crowded early cluster responds to slope. This diagnostic run should distinguish slope-sensitive overlaps from pairs that require temperature or starting-composition changes.
The shallower gradient improved the crowded cluster but incurred a time penalty. Test higher temperature at the original slope to shift selectivity while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Keep the favorable 60 C selectivity and use a shallower gradient to improve the sole unresolved pair. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, allowing full resolution without a time penalty.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so further lengthening is unlikely to help. Raise the starting organic fraction one step to alter early-cluster selectivity while retaining the favorable temperature.

Increasing the starting organic fraction improved the critical pair while preserving separation elsewhere. Test one further step to seek R at least 1.5 for every pair with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep the starting composition and temperature fixed to isolate the effect on the two closest early pairs.

Narrow the gradient window to recover resolution at the shorter duration; the final composition remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution composition. This intermediate slope should restore both critical pairs to R at least 1.5 while remaining faster than injection 6.

With maximum CRF secured, test a higher starting composition for a shorter fully resolved separation. The gentler slope relative to injection 8 may help preserve the early cluster, but the first peaks will need monitoring for compression.

Injection 8 is the fastest fully resolved method so far, but its critical pair has little margin. Lower temperature one step to test whether selectivity improves enough to permit a steeper, faster gradient.

The high-temperature optimum is bracketed closely, with injection 8 retaining maximum CRF. Test the low-temperature extreme for a different elution order that might resolve the early cluster at a steeper slope while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Return to 60 C and test a slope just steeper than the fastest fully resolved method, using a shorter, trimmed gradient. This probes the resolution boundary while keeping the final organic fraction above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Injection 12’s displayed CRF rounds to 1.000, but its critical pair remains below 1.5. Reduce the endpoint one grid step to restore full resolution with a six-minute gradient; the last peak should elute near the gradient end.

The fastest fully resolved method remains injection 8. Test a shallower gradient at the successful starting composition to seek greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and preserving maximum CRF.

At phi0 0.20, only one pair missed the resolution target in the ten-minute gradient. Lengthen it one step to test whether this alternative starting composition can achieve maximum CRF with useful resolution margin.

The remaining critical pair at phi0 0.20 improved from R 1.39 to 1.47 when the gradient was lengthened. One further step should cross 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes, establishing another maximum-CRF method.

Test whether modest cooling at the higher starting composition improves the limiting early pair enough to permit a shorter gradient. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method and the benchmark for this alternative.

Return to the successful starting composition and temperature, with a slope between injections 6 and 14. This should preserve maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 8 while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test an intermediate duration between injections 6 and 14 to refine the tradeoff between speed and resolution margin. This should retain maximum CRF with stronger critical-pair separation than the fastest fully resolved method, injection 8.

Preserve injection 8’s successful gradient slope but end the ramp earlier, testing a shorter programmed gradient. The early critical pairs should retain their resolution; the key check is whether the final hold elutes the last compound before the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 8 to test the nearest faster eight-minute method. This probes the critical-pair resolution boundary; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed method with every pair at R at least 1.5.

The faster neighboring slope failed the resolution threshold, so test one endpoint step below injection 8 for additional separation margin. This should preserve maximum CRF with only a modest increase in last-peak time.

Use a slope between injections 6 and 18 to refine the speed–resolution tradeoff within the maximum-CRF region. This should provide more critical-pair margin than injection 8 while eluting the last compound well before 10 minutes.

Preserve injection 23’s successful slope while trimming the gradient endpoint and duration. This should retain the early-pair resolution margin and maximum CRF, with the final compound eluting near the transition to the hold.

Use injection 23’s proven slope with a lower endpoint that still keeps the last peak inside the gradient, avoiding injection 24’s hold-phase elution. This should retain maximum CRF and R near 1.57 for the critical pair; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
